n: Lower Leg Anatomy and Clinical Correlates

faq.a: It travels in the anterior compartment and must cross the ankle joint to supply the dorsum of the foot.
faq.q: Why does the anterior tibial artery pass anterior to the medial malleolus?

faq.a: Clinical diagnosis: pain on passive stretch, tense swelling, and sensory loss; proceed to urgent fasciotomy.
faq.q: What is the first step if compartment pressure cannot be measured?

faq.a: Diabetic ulcers are deeper, often on pressure points, and may have neuropathic loss; venous ulcers are shallow, above the medial malleolus, with edema.
faq.q: How does a diabetic ulcer differ from a venous ulcer?

exam: A patient with a painful, swollen lower leg after a fracture shows pain on passive ankle dorsiflexion — what diagnosis does this suggest and what is the next urgent step? — Acute compartment syndrome; immediate fasciotomy.

Explain why an ulcer above the medial malleolus in a chronic leg‑swelling patient points to venous disease rather than arterial disease. — Venous ulcers are shallow, irregular, and associated with edema; arterial ulcers are painful, dry, and distal.

A diabetic patient presents with a warm, red lower leg and fever; cultures are unavailable. Which empiric antibiotics are appropriate and why? — Cover Staphylococcus aureus and Gram‑negative bacilli; use a broad‑spectrum penicillin or ceftriaxone, avoiding agents with high nephrotoxicity in renal‑impaired patients.

During examination you cannot palpate the dorsalis pedis pulse but the posterior tibial pulse is present. What does this indicate and what test confirms it? — Possible anterior tibial artery occlusion; confirm with ABI or Doppler if available.

Describe how the saphenous nerve’s course influences wound care on the medial lower leg. — The nerve runs superficially with the great saphenous vein; avoid deep sutures that could injure it and cause sensory loss.
A farmer with chronic leg swelling develops a shallow ulcer; what non‑surgical measures reduce recurrence? — Compression therapy, leg elevation, treat anemia, and control infection.
Why is a fasciotomy performed through two incisions rather than one in the lower leg? — To fully decompress both anterior and lateral compartments and avoid missing hidden pressure pockets.

In a low‑resource setting, how would you assess for peripheral arterial disease without Doppler? — Use ABI with a handheld sphygmomanometer and a handheld Doppler probe; if unavailable, rely on pulse palpation and capillary refill.
ai.title: Lower Leg Anatomy and Clinical Correlates
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The lower leg (crus) contains the anterior, posterior and lateral compartments, each with specific muscles, vessels and nerves. Understanding its layout guides diagnosis of compartment syndrome, ulcers and vascular disease, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Anterior compartment: dorsiflexors, deep peroneal nerve
Posterior compartment: plantar flexors, tibial nerve
Lateral compartment: evertors, superficial peroneal nerve
sections.p: The lower leg extends from the tibial plateau to the ankle joint and is divided into three fascial compartments that house muscles, nerves and vessels.

b: Tibial crest is palpable medially
Fibular head is palpable laterally near the knee
sections.p: The tibia forms the medial border, fibula the lateral border; the interosseous membrane separates them. The deep fascia creates the three compartments.

b: Saphenous vein runs in the superficial fascia of the medial leg, accompanied only by the saphenous nerve
sections.p: Anteriorly the compartments lie deep to the skin and subcutaneous tissue; posteriorly they are covered by the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles.

b: Anterior tibial artery passes anterior to the medial malleolus
Posterior tibial artery passes posterior to the medial malleolus
sections.p: The popliteal artery divides into the anterior tibial artery (anterior compartment) and posterior tibial artery (posterior compartment). The peroneal artery supplies the lateral compartment.

b: Deep peroneal nerve: dorsiflexion, toe extension
Superficial peroneal nerve: eversion, sensation over dorsum
Tibial nerve: plantar flexion, sole sensation
sections.p: The common peroneal nerve splits into deep and superficial branches that run in the anterior and lateral compartments; the tibial nerve descends in the posterior compartment.

b: Anterior compartment: dorsiflexion, foot inversion
Posterior compartment: plantar flexion, foot inversion
Lateral compartment: eversion
sections.p: Muscles of the lower leg produce ankle movements essential for gait, balance and propulsion.

b: Acute compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, tense swelling, pain on passive stretch
Chronic venous ulcer: shallow ulcer above medial malleolus, edema, varicose veins
Diabetic foot infection: often involves the lower leg, may progress to osteomyelitis
sections.p: Compartment syndrome, peripheral arterial disease, venous ulcers and nerve injuries are common problems, especially where trauma, infection and chronic disease are prevalent.

t.b: Is pressure >30 mm Hg indicating compartment syndrome? → >30 mm Hg confirms diagnosis, urgent fasciotomy needed
Is peripheral arterial disease present? → ABI <0.9 suggests arterial insufficiency, need Doppler or duplex if available
What organism is causing ulcer infection? → Guides antibiotic choice; if culture unavailable, treat empirically for Staphylococcus aureus and Gram‑negative bacilli

b: Inspect for swelling, discoloration, ulceration
Palpate compartments for firmness; compare both sides
Check distal pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial)
Test sensation in the web space (deep peroneal) and lateral foot (superficial peroneal)
Assess active dorsiflexion and plantar flexion against resistance
sections.p: A systematic bedside exam of the lower leg quickly identifies compartment syndrome, vascular compromise and nerve injury.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe, rapidly increasing leg pain with tense swelling
Absent distal pulses with cold foot
Rapidly spreading cellulitis with systemic signs
